newsitem.title: USA: US lawmakers urge panel to drop SPR sale from bill. [CORRECTED 1:31 GMT 10/9]
newsitem.headline: US lawmakers urge panel to drop SPR sale from bill. [CORRECTED 1:31 GMT 10/9]

text.p: Three U.S. Congressmen Wednesday urged the House Rules Committee to remove provisions to sell oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve from a spending bill the full House will consider later this week.

Reps. John Dingell, a Michigan Democrat, and Republicans Dan Schaefer of Colorado and Billy Tauzin of Louisiana, spoke against the Appropriations Committee's plan to sell $209 million from the reserve, and another proposal to sell $89.5 million of SPR oil to fund the National Endowment for the Arts.
The measures were being considered in the fiscal 1998 $13 billion Interior spending bill for national parks, programs for Native Americans, and land and resource management programs.
Schaefer, who chairs the House Commerce subcommittee that oversees the SPR, said the measures would violate House rules because the authorizing committee had not approved them.
The Appropriations Committee's bill, which the full House is to consider later this week, called for selling $209 million of SPR oil to cover the reserve's operating costs.

Rep. Sidney Yates, an Illinois Democrat, was pushing an amendment to sell an additional $89.5 million of SPR oil to restore funds for the National Endowment for the Arts that the Appropriations Committee slashed from the Interior spending bill.
The Rules Committee was locked in a battle between Republicans, who wanted to close down the NEA, and Democrats who wanted a chance to vote on Yates' amendment to keep it operating for another year.
Even if the Rules Committee allows a vote on Yates' amendment, Schaefer told reporters it likely would be challenged, and funding beside the SPR sale likely would have to be found.
The Rules Committee was expected to vote on the measures late Wednesday or Thursday.
Schaefer succeeded last year in getting the Rules Committee to strike out an SPR oil sale from the House bill, but the sale was restored when the House and Senate bills were meshed in conference.
